title: Free will and decree
hook: two verses side by side, and the theologians who tried to hold them both

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shia theology, and your line: justice and guidance. Were you fair to someone who didn't expect it? Today, the question that runs under this whole part. Day one thousand two hundred forty-nine.

The caliph Umar is on the road to Syria with his companions when word comes: plague has broken out in the land ahead. He asks for advice, hears his advisers disagree, and decides to turn back. Abu Ubayda, a companion of the Prophet, objects. Are you running from the decree of Allah? Umar's answer is in Sahih al-Bukhari: yes, we run from the decree of Allah to the decree of Allah. If your camels came down into a valley with one green side and one bare one, he asks, wouldn't you graze them by Allah's decree whichever side you chose? In the schools of theology this became a hard question. If Allah decrees everything, what's left for my choice? And if my choice is real, what's left for His decree? Today, the knot.
screen: `PLAGUE AHEAD.` → `FROM DECREE TO DECREE.` → `WHAT'S LEFT FOR ME?`

segments.voice: Start with two verses, in Pickthall's translation. One says: "Then whosoever will, let him believe, and whosoever will, let him disbelieve." That sounds like a real choice, handed to us. Another says: "Yet ye will not, unless Allah willeth." That sounds like every choice rests inside His will. The Qur'an puts both on the page and doesn't apologize for either. The theologians we've met in this part each tried to hold them together. The Mu'tazilah leaned hard on the first. A just God, they said, only judges people for acts that are truly their own, so humans bring their acts into being. The Ash'aris leaned on another verse: "When Allah hath created you and what ye make?" Allah creates every act, they said, and the human being acquires it, takes it on, and is answerable for it. Their word for this is kasb, acquisition. The Maturidis said Allah creates the act, and the human being's free choice is real, and it's that choice that is judged. And Shia theology has a saying it traces to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq: neither compulsion nor complete handing over, but a matter between the two. Each school ties the same knot its own way. None of them says we're puppets, and none of them says Allah steps aside. Each one is trying to keep both verses true at once. And Umar's answer at the edge of the plague is a version anyone can use: even choosing the green side of the valley sits inside the decree. Do your part with your whole effort. Then let the outcome rest with Allah.
screen: `WHOSOEVER WILL, LET HIM BELIEVE.` · `YE WILL NOT, UNLESS ALLAH WILLETH.` · `KASB, AND A MATTER BETWEEN THE TWO.` · then, large: `DO YOUR PART. LET IT REST.`

segments.voice: The practice: make a free choice for good. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one small good thing you could do today. A message you've been putting off. A dish someone else usually washes. Choose it now, on purpose, the way Umar chose his road. Feel the choosing. Then picture the moment after you've done it, and let go of how it lands. Whether they answer the message, whether anyone notices. That part isn't yours to hold. If you pray, you can hand the outcome to Allah in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Free will and decree. How human choice and Allah's decree fit together: a question the schools answer in different ways, each keeping both true. Today's word.
Your line: choose, and trust. Today, do the good thing you chose, fully, then leave the result where it belongs. Tomorrow, why suffering? Day one thousand two hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims affirm both Allah's decree and human responsibility, and the schools of theology explain how they fit in different ways, from the Ash'ari teaching of kasb to the Shia saying of 'a matter between the two'.

fork.setup: you're Umar. plague is in the land ahead, and a companion asks: are you running from the decree of Allah? what do you say?
options: no, I'll go on; whatever is decreed will happen.
yes: from the decree of Allah to the decree of Allah.
decree has nothing to do with it.
fork.reveal: in Sahih al-Bukhari, Umar runs from decree to decree, like a herder choosing the green side of a valley over the bare one.

original.note: Arabic: acquisition, earning; the Ash'ari term for how a person takes on an act.
